title: Sunday schools
hookLine: Robert Raikes starts schools on Sundays for children working in factories the rest of the week
last: YOU CANNOT SAY YOU DID NOT KNOW.

lines: THE MACHINES GO QUIET ON SUNDAY.
cards: One day a week, the machines in an English factory town go quiet, and the children who work them are out in the streets: loud, ragged, bored, getting into fights, with no school to go to and no one to stop them.
Neighbors complain. A newspaper man in Gloucester, Robert Raikes, looks at the same children and asks a different question. Not how do we keep them quiet, but what if they could read?

teach.b: Today Sunday school can mean a cheerful hour of Bible stories while the grown-ups are in church. It began as something tougher. Raikes's children worked during the week.
Sunday was their only free day, so Sunday was the only day they could learn.
He found women in the neighborhood who could teach, paid them, and opened classes in their homes. The children learned to read and to spell, and the book they read from was the Bible.
They learned the catechism and went to church. They also, the accounts say, had to come with clean hands and combed hair.
Raikes owned a newspaper, so he wrote about it, and the idea spread from town to town and across the sea. Tradition gives him the credit, though others had started Sunday classes before him.
Behind it was a conviction that sounds obvious now and wasn't then: a poor child working in a factory was worth teaching.
In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo children away, Jesus is displeased and says: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God."
In King James English, suffer means let. Let them come. Not everyone liked it.
Some people worried that teaching poor children to read would make them restless. Raikes kept the schools going anyway.
To him, reading was a gift, not a danger.

how: Churches of different denominations hold Sunday school classes for children, and often for adults too, usually before or during the main service.

games.q: you're Raikes. on Sunday the factory children run wild in the streets, and neighbors complain. what do you do?
o: ask the town to keep them indoors on Sundays.

games.why: he paid neighborhood women to teach them to read, using the Bible, and wrote about it in his newspaper until the idea spread.

practice: Bring to mind a child you know, your own, a niece, a neighbor, a student, or the child you used to be, and one small thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, how to fold a paper boat, a line of a song or a psalm.
Think how you'd show it, slowly, one step at a time. If you pray, pray for that child by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
